chapter.title: Three activation choices
chapter.question: How do sigmoid, ReLU and linear activations differ?
chapter.narration: The activation decides the shape of the output, not the input.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

presentation.why: The existing card renderer owns the layout and motion.

nodes.title: Sigmoid
nodes.body: Squashes any real-valued score through 1/(1+e^-z) into a bounded S-curve between 0 and 1, so outputs can be read as probabilities.

nodes.title: ReLU
nodes.body: Passes positive scores through unchanged and clamps negatives to zero, producing a hinge at the origin; the range runs from 0 to infinity.

nodes.title: Linear
nodes.body: Returns the score untouched, so the output follows a straight line with no ceiling or floor; the range is unbounded and used for regression.

visual.takeaway: The activation decides the shape of the output, not the input.

chapter.title: Compute one example
chapter.question: What are the exact steps for these numbers?
chapter.narration: Scale, add the bias, squash: that is one forward pass.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

presentation.why: The existing card renderer owns the layout and motion.

nodes.title: 1. Scale
nodes.body: Multiply the input by its weight: 2 × 0.7 = 1.4. The product is the first quantity carried into the sum.

nodes.title: 2. Add bias
nodes.body: Add the remaining weighted input and the bias: 1.4 − 0.5 + 0.3 = 1.2. This is the score before activation.

nodes.title: 3. Squash
nodes.body: Pass the score through sigma: σ(1.2) = 0.77. The bounded result is the output for this forward pass.

visual.takeaway: Scale, add the bias, squash: that is one forward pass.

chapter.title: The forward pass
chapter.question: What does the neuron do as an algorithm?
chapter.narration: One forward pass: no weights change.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

presentation.why: The existing card renderer owns the layout and motion.

nodes.title: Read inputs
nodes.body: Load the input vector x, every weight w and the bias b, so the pass begins from a fully known state.

nodes.title: Compute z
nodes.body: Multiply each input by its weight, sum the products, then add the bias to reach the pre-activation value z = 1.2.

nodes.title: Return y
nodes.body: Send z through the activation to get y = 0.77, then return that output unchanged, because no weights move.

visual.takeaway: One forward pass: no weights change.

chapter.title: How the idea evolved
chapter.question: Where did this model come from?
chapter.narration: The idea moved from one unit to a trainable network.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

presentation.why: The existing card renderer owns the layout and motion.

nodes.title: Perceptron
nodes.body: 1958: the first trainable unit. It adjusted its weights from labelled examples until it could separate classes with a linear boundary.

nodes.title: Backpropagation
nodes.body: 1986: backpropagation made credit assignment practical, letting multi-layer networks learn from error and tune their hidden layers.

nodes.title: Scale
nodes.body: Today: scale, deep networks and hardware let the same idea train on far more data and far larger models than a single unit.

visual.takeaway: The idea moved from one unit to a trainable network.

chapter.title: Remember the three moves
chapter.question: How can I remember what a neuron does?
chapter.narration: Weight, sum, activate: the three moves of a neuron.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

presentation.why: The existing card renderer owns the layout and motion.

nodes.title: Weight
nodes.body: Each input is scaled by its connection weight, so stronger signals count for more.

nodes.title: Sum
nodes.body: The weighted inputs are added into one score, pooling the evidence before activation.

nodes.title: Activate
nodes.body: The score is transformed into the output, turning the weighted evidence into a result.

visual.takeaway: Weight, sum, activate: the three moves of a neuron.
